Although neither Samsung nor Google offer industry-leading battery capacities, it’s fair to say that we’ve never been left that disappointed with their abilities. While we’re yet to review the Galaxy S26 FE, it shares the same 4900mAh capacity as last year’s Galaxy S25 FE which we concluded could see us through a busy day before needing a top-up overnight. 

Pixel 10a. Image Credit (Trusted Reviews)

It’s a similar story with the Pixel 10a as, although it has a slightly larger 5100mAh battery, it offers a similar all-day life before needing a recharge overnight. 

So, while you probably shouldn’t expect either to offer two-day life (unless you are an extremely light user), both the Galaxy S26 FE and Pixel 10a should see you through a busy day.

## Battery Life and Charging

##### Google is the first to add magnetic wireless charging in the Android world

Battery life and charging speeds might be simillar, but it's nice to have magnets! | Image by PhoneArena.

The Pixel 10 carries a significant battery capacity advantage, with 4,970 mAh vs the Galaxy S25’s 4,000 mAh. We expect that to result in better battery life from the Pixel, especially with the custom-built Tensor G 5 chip inside. Google claims 30+ hours of use on a charge.

Charging is also an area where the Pixel 10 stands out. Now it supports Qi2 magnetic wireless charging with Google’s Pixelsnap ecosystem of chargers and stands. Samsung sticks to standard 15W wireless charging without magnets.

title: Samsung Galaxy S26 Plus Vs Pixel 10 Pro XL Real-World Battery Test - 24x7Report
text:
### In summary:

- Tech Advisor conducted real-world battery tests comparing the Samsung Galaxy S26+ and Google Pixel 10 Pro XL under identical usage conditions.
- The Galaxy S26+ significantly outperformed the Pixel 10 Pro XL, lasting 26 hours versus approximately 11-12 hours during intensive testing.
- For users prioritizing all-day battery life, the S26+ proves superior for extended use with GPS, social media, and multimedia activities.

...

Google, for example, estimates that the new Pixel 10 Pro XL should last for 24 hours. Samsung notes that the Galaxy S26+ should last for 31 hours of continuous video streaming. Both brands include a caveat that essentially says: it depends on how you use the phone. Also, you might need to enable battery saver mode and turn the brightness down.

...

These apps don’t drain the battery much and are not processor-intensive.

...

Just like when I was in Grein the day

...

However, this wasn’t meant to be a benchmark test – I simply wanted to use the S26+ as I normally would all day and see if it kept running until the late evening. 

Surprisingly, the S26+ seriously outperformed the Pixel 10 Pro XL. By the afternoon, the phone was at 40%. It wasn’t in battery saver mode and the screen was still at full brightness. 

After dinner, the phone had dropped to 30% and was still chugging along at 25% by 10pm that night. In the morning, the S26+ lasted for another five hours! Fittingly, the S26+ lasted a full 26 hours.

## Which is the battery life champion?

I decided to retest the Pixel 10 Pro XL as a sanity check. Using the phone all day to take photos, listen to music, and for GPS routing, I duplicated the results. The Pixel 10 Pro XL lasted about 11 hours again. I also retested the S26+ for another full day and it lasted until lunch again the next day (admittedly, it simply sat on a table all night).

In the end, the Samsung Galaxy S26+ was the battery life champion. The phone lasted over 24 hours while the Google Pixel 10 Pro XL lasted only about 11-12 hours. It means I’d be much more likely to use the S26+ if the goal is to make a phone last all day – and then some.

# I’ve tested the iPhone 17e, Pixel 10a, and Galaxy A57 — here’s the sub-$700 mid-range phone worth buying
Face Off
By John Velasco
Published 13 November 2026
They all got price increases
(Image credit: John Velasco / Tom's Guide)
* Specs
* Camera Samples
* iPhone 17e
* Pixel 10a
* Galaxy A57
* Verdict
Just like most other consumer electronics, the price of mid-range phones has increased substantially over the course of the last year. They’re still largely considered "budget," especially when many of the best phones and best foldables easily cost $1,299+.
Mid-range phones quite simply offer the right balance between features and performance. For my next face-off, I’m putting the iPhone 17e, Pixel 10a, and Galaxy A57 to the test to tell you exactly which one’s worth getting if you have $700 to spend.
I’ve personally tested all three of them over the last six months, so I’ll tell you how their cameras perform, how fast they charge, how their batteries hold up, and what software features they offer.

## iPhone 17e vs. Pixel 10a vs. Galaxy A57: Camera samples
Image 1 of 24
Apple iPhone 17e. (Image credit: John Velasco / Tom's Guide) Google Pixel 10a. (Image credit: John Velasco / Tom's Guide) ## Apple iPhone 17e
(Image credit: Tom's Guide / John Velasco)
As I said in my review, “the iPhone 17e feels more like what the iPhone 16e should’ve been from the start.” It’s also the most affordable option in Apple’s lineup if you’re looking to spend as little as possible, offering a well-rounded experience that gets the job done.
Just as before, though, Apple’s kept just a single camera on the back — which is unheard of in an era where practically everything has a dual-camera setup. But despite this shortcoming, the iPhone 17e’s 48MP main camera performs brilliantly across challenging lighting conditions. From the sharp details and definition it pulls out, to how it neutralizes hotspots in bright scenes, it doesn’t disappoint. It’s also a master of low light, proving to me it’s the best camera phone of the bunch in terms of raw performance.
(Image credit: Tom's Guide / John Velasco)
Under the hood, it’s easily the powerhouse of this trio. Thanks to Apple’s A19 silicon, the iPhone 17e delivers superior CPU and GPU performance that keeps everyday multitasking snappy and handles demanding, graphically-intensive games far better than its Android counterparts. I appreciate that Apple also made a couple of smart hardware upgrades — like bumping starting storage to a generous 256GB and finally adding MagSafe support.
(Image credit: Tom's Guide / John Velasco)
That said, the iPhone 17e isn’t without a few glaring compromises. Holding onto a 60Hz display feels increasingly dated when 120Hz panels have become standard across the rest of the mid-range market — and the lack of an ultrawide camera means it’s not as suitable for sprawling landscapes and group photos.
And while iOS 27 brings some much-needed new features, like the ability to create custom passes and use generative AI with its Reframe tool to shift to a new perspective for photos, Siri AI remains functionally inferior compared to Gemini. While the assistant is more proactive with what I’m doing on the phone to offer actionable recommendations — like creating a reminder when someone texts me about an upcoming event — Siri AI lacks the deeper third-party app support that lets it work across more apps.
Worst of all, its recent price hike to $699 (up from its $599 launch price) makes those omissions much harder to overlook.
## Google Pixel 10a
(Image credit: Tom's Guide / John Velasco) (Image credit: Tom's Guide / John Velasco)
There’s good and bad with the Pixel 10a. Just like the iPhone 17e, the design makes it look like a generic slab — but at least Google’s made the camera housing completely flush and offers some fun color options. Despite these design tweaks, the phone is by and large similar to its predecessor, the Pixel 9a, including how it packs the same Tensor G4 chip as before.
Its 6.3-inch Actua display is surprisingly sharp and bright, besting its rivals with a peak brightness of 1,896 nits in our lab testing. Even better, it posted the longest battery life of the trio with an average of 15 hours and 16 minutes. Better yet, it also delivers the fastest wired charging times we’ve tested — reaching 64% in 30 minutes.
Where the Pixel 10a truly separates itself, though, is on the software front. Gemini remains leagues ahead of Siri AI and Bixby, especially in its ability to execute complex, multi-step actions across different apps. I’m not simply referring to asking it to check upcoming New York Knicks home games and add them to my calendar — I’m talking about everyday things like ordering Dunkin’ Donuts through DoorDash, all with a simple voice command.
(Image credit: Future)
If that’s not enough, the Pixel 10a really widens the software divide with how practically the Pixel desktop mode works when I connect it to an external monitor, turning the phone into a surprisingly capable workstation when I happen to leave my work laptop at home. Even on the photography side, new AI tools like Auto Best Take and Camera Coach help you nail group shots and framing without any heavy lifting.
(Image credit: Tom's Guide / John Velasco)
However, Google’s decision to reuse the same Tensor G4 chip as its predecessor puts it at a major disadvantage in raw CPU and GPU benchmarking compared to the iPhone 17e. And in 2026, having a base storage of 128GB feels stingy. Even though the camera performance is better than most other mid-range phones, I’m disappointed that there's barely any improvement over its predecessor — a tougher pill to swallow now that its $100 price hike has pushed it to $599.
## Samsung Galaxy A57
(Image credit: Future) (Image credit: Future) (Image credit: Future) (Image credit: Future) (Image credit: Future)
Out of the bunch, the Samsung Galaxy A57 has the most premium look and feel — rivaling its flagship sibling, the Galaxy S26. Not only does it combine the glass-meets-metal build Samsung’s known to give its top-tier models, but it also manages to have an IP68 rating.
If you prefer a phone with a larger screen to see more of what you’re doing or stream your favorite shows while on the go, the Galaxy A57’s massive 6.7-inch Super AMOLED display with a 120Hz refresh rate doesn’t disappoint. It’s way bigger than the 6.1- and 6.3-inch screens of the iPhone 17e and Pixel 10a, respectively.
(Image credit: Tom's Guide / Stephen Lambrechts)
Another notable feature is how it’s the only phone in this trio to pack a triple-camera system on the back, pairing a 50MP main sensor with a 12MP ultrawide and a 5MP macro lens. While that dedicated macro shooter feels more like a forced addition just to give it the upper hand, having three distinct lenses nonetheless gives you extra shooting versatility that neither the iPhone 17e nor the Pixel 10a can match.
Throw in some S26-level Galaxy AI features — like access to object eraser and a voice transcription tool — and it has a robust toolset to help save you time. I also love how it caters to power users like myself, with the ability to run two apps side by side, which neither the iPhone 17e nor the Pixel 10a can do.
(Image credit: Tom's Guide / Stephen Lambrechts)
Where the Galaxy A57 stumbles, though, is under the hood. Powered by Samsung’s Exynos 1680 chip, it posted the lowest performance scores of the bunch in our testing, lagging behind both the Pixel 10a and especially the iPhone 17e. Worse yet, it doesn’t even have the luxury of wireless charging — a glaring omission, in my opinion, now that its $50 price hike has pushed the cost up to $599.

## iPhone 17e vs. Pixel 10a vs. Galaxy A57: Bottom line
(Image credit: John Velasco / Tom's Guide)
If there’s one I’d buy with my own money, it has to be the Pixel 10a — with the iPhone 17e not too far behind it. That’s because Google’s mid-range phone checks off more of the boxes on my list than the other two.
All three phones got price hikes, but the Pixel 10a’s $599 price tag is easier to swallow than the iPhone 17e’s heftier $699 cost. And while the Galaxy A57 matches the Pixel’s price point, its weak processing performance combined with flat camera results aren’t enough to prove to me it offers better value at the same price.
Ultimately, the Google Pixel 10a is the mid-range phone I recommend. I can’t stress enough the value of its software package alone — and backed up by seven years’ worth of major Android and security updates, it’s undeniably the smartest long-term investment you can make in the mid-range market right now.

title: Pixel 11 Beats Galaxy S26? $799 Verdict [2026]
text:
The second trade-off favors Samsung. Engadget states that the Galaxy S26 Ultra has longer battery life and faster charging than the Pixel 11 Pro XL. Battery stamina is one of the most common reasons people pick a phone, and heavy users feel it every day. A phone that lasts through a long shift and refills quickly removes a daily source of friction.

...

Samsung’s own listing describes the Galaxy S26 as 7.2 mm thick and 167 g, with a 4,300 mAh battery. It cites up to 30 hours of video playback and up to 55% charge in around 30 minutes, so the 31 hours in this article’s title applies to the larger models rather than the base S26. The Galaxy S26+ steps up to a 6.7-inch display, a 50 MP camera, and a 4,900 mAh typical battery capacity, with up to 31 hours of video playback.

...

One caveat applies to every Samsung figure here. Video playback hours and charge percentages come from the manufacturer’s own testing conditions, and real-world results swing with screen brightness, signal strength and app mix. The same caution applies to Google’s figures. Neither company’s headline number is a guarantee, and Engadget’s hands-on comparison carries more weight for the Ultra versus Pro XL matchup than any spec sheet.

...

| Spec | Google Pixel 11 | Samsung Galaxy S26 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Reveal or announcement | August 2026 | February 25, 2026 |
| Chip | Google Tensor G6 | Not confirmed |
| RAM | 12 GB | 12 GB |
| Display | 6.3-inch Actua, 3,000 nits peak | 6.3-inch (S26+ is 6.7-inch) |
| Storage | 256 GB or 512 GB | 256 GB or 512 GB |
| Battery | 30+ hours of battery life | 4,300 mAh, up to 30 hours video playback |
| Fast charging | Not confirmed for base model | Up to 55% in around 30 minutes |
| Weight and thickness | Not confirmed | 167 g, 7.2 mm |
| U.S. price | $899 launch price | From $899.99 before trade-in |

...

## Battery Life and Charging: Where Samsung Wins

Engadget gives Samsung the clear win on endurance at the top of both lineups. The Galaxy S26 Ultra has longer battery life and faster charging than the Pixel 11 Pro XL, per the outlet. For people who run navigation, video calls and hotspot duty all day, that matchup may settle the question alone.

The raw spec sheets add some nuance but also some tension. Google lists the Pixel 11 Pro with wired charging up to 75% in about 30 minutes. Samsung lists the base Galaxy S26 at up to 55% in around 30 minutes. Read quickly, that looks like a Pixel advantage. Yet Engadget says the Ultra charges faster than the Pro XL, and the Ultra’s own charging figure does not appear in the verified material.

The resolution is that these numbers compare different models under different test conditions. A base-model S26 figure tells you little about the Ultra, and a Pro figure tells you little about the Pro XL. The only direct head-to-head in the supplied reporting is Engadget’s Ultra versus Pro XL call. Buyers should lean on that one and treat cross-model spec comparisons as rough hints at best.

Battery life also depends on habits. A Pixel 11 or Pixel 11 Pro that lists 30+ hours will carry most people through a normal day. The Galaxy S26 cites up to 30 hours of video playback and the S26+ cites up to 31 hours. On paper, the base phones land close together. The gap Engadget describes shows up at the Ultra and Pro XL tier, so it matters most to buyers shopping the top shelf.
